query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During prolonged high‐temperature exposure, the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy degrades primarily because oxygen (or low oxygen potential in reducing gases) promotes the formation of brittle oxide phases (predominantly Al‐ and Ti‐oxides) that segregate to grain boundaries. This localized oxidation weakens intergranular cohesion and concentrates stress, leading eventually to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured alloy with a fine, nearly single‐phase FCC matrix featuring clean, ductile grain boundaries and minimal pre‐existing oxide or secondary phase precipitates.
generation.intervention: Perform a series of elevated-temperature (650–750 °C) exposures under carefully controlled atmospheres that are either oxidizing (e.g., O2-rich) or reducing (e.g., H2/Ar mixtures) while keeping temperature and time constant.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures between 650 °C and 750 °C for durations up to 100 hours. The gas environment is varied by controlling oxygen partial pressure from high (oxidizing) to low (reducing) levels.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and segregation of Al- and Ti-rich oxide phases along grain boundaries (or within intergranular regions) that disrupt the continuity of the ductile FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperatures accelerate the selective oxidation of reactive elements (Al and Ti) at grain boundaries. In oxidizing atmospheres, a continuous (or near-continuous) brittle oxide film forms. In reducing atmospheres, although the external oxidation is suppressed, internal oxygen penetration may still drive localized oxide precipitation. In both cases, these oxide features act as stress concentrators, impede dislocation motion, and embrittle the microstructure, ultimately leading to intergranular fracture and catastrophic failure under mechanical or thermal loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-manufactured baseline, samples exposed in oxidizing conditions will show significant grain boundary decoration with brittle oxides, reduced ductility, and lower failure strain. Samples in reducing conditions may show less extensive surface oxide formation yet manifest internal oxidation markers and similar, though potentially delayed, embrittlement. Catastrophic failure is expected to correlate with the density and connectivity of these oxide phases.
generation.baseline: The initial additively manufactured alloy with an intact FCC microstructure and ductile grain boundaries, before any significant exposure to high-temperature reactive gases.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is considered relevant for service conditions at temperatures between 650 °C and 750 °C and exposure times sufficient for oxidation kinetics (up to 100 hours); deviations outside these bounds may invoke different degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain to what extent each oxide type (Al2O3 vs TiO2) dominates the embrittlement process and whether residual stresses from the additive manufacturing process may synergistically accelerate oxide formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy samples with identical initial microstructures. Expose them at 700 °C for up to 100 hours under two atmosphere types: one with high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) and another with a reducing environment (controlled H2/Ar mix). After exposure, perform detailed microstructural analysis (using TEM/EDS and EBSD) to quantify the extent, location, and continuity of oxide phase precipitation along grain boundaries. Concurrently, assess mechanical integrity via standardized fracture toughness/tensile tests.
measurements: Area fraction and continuity of oxide films along grain boundaries (via high-resolution TEM/EDS)
Mechanical property degradation (fracture toughness, tensile ductility)
Time to catastrophic failure under low-strain rate mechanical loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-exposure microstructural analyses do not reveal a significant increase in segregated oxide phases along grain boundaries—i.e. if the oxide formation remains minimal or non-contiguous—and if the mechanical properties do not degrade relative to the as-manufactured baseline in either gas environment, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary oxidation governs degradation and catastrophic failure is falsified.

Corrosion behavior

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy [2] . Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion [2] .

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
